front_blocks.md: Define **chemical shift**.

back_blocks.md: A **chemical shift** (δ, in ppm) is the position of a peak on an NMR spectrum, measured relative to the TMS reference peak at 0 ppm, indicating the electronic environment of the atom.

cards.back_md: A **chemical shift** (δ, in ppm) is the position of a peak on an NMR spectrum, measured relative to the TMS reference peak at 0 ppm, indicating the electronic environment of the atom.

front_blocks.md: What is the reference compound used in <sup>13</sup>C NMR, and what solvent is typically used to dissolve the sample?

back_blocks.md: The reference compound is **tetramethylsilane (TMS)**, set at 0 ppm. The sample is dissolved in **CDCl****<sub>3</sub>** (deuterochloroform), whose solvent peak at 77 ppm can be ignored.

front_blocks.md: **True or False?**
In <sup>13</sup>C NMR, the height of each signal is proportional to the number of carbon atoms in that environment.

back_blocks.md: **False.** In <sup>**13**</sup>**C NMR**, the height of each signal is **not** proportional to the number of carbon atoms. Each non-equivalent carbon produces one signal regardless of how many carbons share that environment.

front_blocks.md: A carbonyl carbon (C=O in a ketone or aldehyde) gives a <sup>13</sup>C NMR signal in the range **..........**  ppm, while an sp<sup>3</sup> alkyl carbon gives a signal in the range **..........**  ppm.

front_blocks.md: How many <sup>13</sup>C NMR signals does propanone produce, and why?

back_blocks.md: **Propanone** produces **2 signals**: one for the **carbonyl carbon** (200 ppm) and one for the **two equivalent methyl carbons** (30 ppm). The two CH<sub>3</sub> groups are in identical environments due to the molecule's symmetry.

front_blocks.md: Define **carbon-13 NMR spectroscopy**.

back_blocks.md: **Carbon-13 NMR spectroscopy** is an analytical technique that detects distinct <sup>13</sup>C environments in a molecule to determine molecular structure, producing one signal per type of non-equivalent carbon.

cards.back_md: **Carbon-13 NMR spectroscopy** is an analytical technique that detects distinct <sup>13</sup>C environments in a molecule to determine molecular structure, producing one signal per type of non-equivalent carbon.

front_blocks.md: **True or False?**
<sup>13</sup>C NMR spectra show splitting patterns similar to those seen in <sup>1</sup>H NMR spectra.

back_blocks.md: **False.** <sup>**13**</sup>**C NMR** spectra show **sharp single signals** with no complicated splitting patterns, unlike <sup>1</sup>H NMR where spin-spin splitting produces multiplets.

back_blocks.md: A carbon bonded to oxygen (sp<sup>3</sup>, next to oxygen) gives a <sup>13</sup>C signal in the range **50-70 ppm**.

back_blocks.md: In <sup>13</sup>C NMR, only **carbon-13** carbon atoms produce signals. The more abundant **carbon-12** carbon atoms are NMR-inactive and do not appear on the spectrum.

front_blocks.md: Define **equivalent carbons**.

back_blocks.md: **Equivalent carbons** are carbon atoms in identical molecular environments due to symmetry, producing a single <sup>13</sup>C NMR signal rather than separate signals for each carbon.

cards.back_md: **Equivalent carbons** are carbon atoms in identical molecular environments due to symmetry, producing a single <sup>13</sup>C NMR signal rather than separate signals for each carbon.

front_blocks.md: How many <sup>13</sup>C NMR peaks does benzene produce, and why?

back_blocks.md: **Benzene** produces **1 peak** because all six carbon atoms are equivalent due to the molecule's multiple lines of symmetry — they all occupy the same molecular environment.

front_blocks.md: **True or False?**
Propan-2-ol gives more <sup>13</sup>C NMR peaks than propan-1-ol.

back_blocks.md: **False.** **Propan-2-ol** gives **2 peaks** (the two equivalent CH<sub>3</sub> groups are symmetric). **Propan-1-ol** gives **3 peaks** (no equivalent carbons). Propan-2-ol gives fewer peaks.

front_blocks.md: To predict the number of <sup>13</sup>C NMR peaks, first look for **..........**  in the molecule. Carbons that are equivalent due to symmetry produce a **..........**  signal.

back_blocks.md: To predict the number of <sup>13</sup>C NMR peaks, first look for **symmetry** in the molecule. Carbons that are equivalent due to symmetry produce a **single** signal.

front_blocks.md: How many <sup>13</sup>C NMR peaks would you predict for 1,3-dihydroxybenzene, and how are they determined?

back_blocks.md: **1,3-Dihydroxybenzene** gives **4 peaks**. The molecule has a plane of symmetry, making some ring carbons equivalent. Counting unique environments — two types of C–OH, one C between them and one equivalent pair of unsubstituted carbons — gives 4.

front_blocks.md: Define **molecular environment (****<sup>13</sup>****C NMR)**.

back_blocks.md: A **molecular environment** in <sup>13</sup>C NMR is the unique chemical surroundings of a carbon atom; non-equivalent carbons in different environments appear as separate peaks on the spectrum.

cards.back_md: A **molecular environment** in <sup>13</sup>C NMR is the unique chemical surroundings of a carbon atom; non-equivalent carbons in different environments appear as separate peaks on the spectrum.

front_blocks.md: **True or False?**
A molecule with five carbon atoms must always show five peaks in its <sup>13</sup>C NMR spectrum.

back_blocks.md: **False.** A molecule with five carbons shows **at most** five peaks, but if some carbons are equivalent due to symmetry, fewer peaks are observed.

front_blocks.md: Why is counting the number of <sup>13</sup>C NMR resonances a useful first step in analysing an unknown spectrum?

back_blocks.md: It immediately tells you the number of **distinct carbon environments**, which can distinguish between structural isomers — for example, the three isomers of dihydroxybenzene each have a different number of environments.
